paper_title: Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM agents are commonly trained with RLVR, but the sparse nature of typical RLVR rewards makes credit assignment challenging, especially for long-horizon tasks. We propose Self-Credit, an end-to-end agentic RL method that creates dense supervision signals from sparse outcome rewards using self-generated credit assignment via intra-group rescaling. Self-Credit builds on group-based RL with three components. First, during its rollouts, the policy model generates summaries with citations to earlier turns containing critical evidence, which serve as self-generated credit. Second, we refine this model-generated credit with intra-group rescaling, which compares cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt. This approach uses group-level agreement and disagreement to remove undeserved credit and further emphasize credit assigned to critical actions. Third, advantage reweighting uses the rescaled credit weights to update the advantages of the cited turns. On BrowseComp-Plus, Self-Credit improves over the base models by 37.0 and 36.2 points on Qwen3 8B and 32B respectively, and outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines by 8.5 and 5.6 points, respectively. Self-Credit also improves over the strongest baselines by 4.9 points on GAIA and 4.7 points on xBench-DeepSearch. Analyses show that self-generated credit provides useful signals for selecting critical actions, and that intra-group rescaling, especially on failed rollouts, is important across model scales.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly used for agentic tasks, where they interact with environments and issue tool calls as actions. principal challenge in building long-horizon agents is the nature of supervision: typically, models are trained via RLVR using only sparse rewards (Guo et al., 2025), as additional dense supervision is expensive to define and collect (Tao et al., 2025; Setlur et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a,e). Recent work extends standard RLVR algorithms to provide credit assignment even when only sparse rewards are available, including approaches that use external judges (Zhang et al., 2026b; Zeng et al., 2025) and learned critics (Zhang et al., 2025d; Shi et al., 2026). However, these methods usually require additional supervision signals and often suffer from context growth in challenging long-horizon tasks (Sun et al., 2025). Figure 1 Self-Credit leverages self-generated summaries with Intragroup rescaling to provide credit assignment for long-horizon agentic RL. Self-Credit outperforms strong baselines on challenging long-horizon tasks, such as BrowseComp-Plus. 1 Inspired by context management methods for LLM agents (Li et al., 2026b; Xie et al., 2026), we propose Self-Credit, novel agentic RL method in which the policy LLM agent performs credit assignment through compaction using self-generated credit with intra-group rescaling. As illustrated in Figure 1, Self-Credit builds on standard group-based RL algorithm with three components to create dense supervision signals from single sparse outcome reward. First, we prompt the policy model to generate summary with citations that identify earlier turns in the interaction history containing critical evidence for the agentic task. The summaries are used for compaction to compress the long context, and the citations serve as self-generated credit. Second, intra-group rescaling refines this credit by comparing cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt. In particular, this rescaling uses agreement and disagreement across the entire rollout group to determine how to remove undeserved credit and further emphasize credit assigned to critical actions, grounding the credit weights in group-level statistics. Third, advantage reweighting uses the rescaled credit weights to selectively strengthen the advantages of tokens in model-cited turns to emphasize important behaviors in long trajectory. We evaluate Self-Credit on challenging long-horizon search and retrieval tasks, including multi-hop QA on BrowseComp-Plus and deep research on GAIA and xBench-DeepSearch. As shown in Figure 1, on BrowseComp-Plus, Self-Credit improves over the Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B base agents by 37.0 and 36.2 percentage points, respectively, and outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines by 8.5 and 5.6 points, respectively. On deep research tasks, Self-Credit also outperforms the strongest evaluated baselines by 4.9 points on GAIA and 4.7 points on xBench-DeepSearch. Ablations show that intra-group credit rescaling, especially downweighting repeated turns shared across failed rollouts, is important across model scales, and that using self-generated credit provides more effective credit assignment than the alternatives. Further analyses show that self-generated citations identify important actions related to gold answers, and that intra-group rescaling rules are applied selectively during training at higher selection quality than baselines. Our main contributions are as follows: (1) We introduce Self-Credit, an end-to-end RL algorithm for training long-horizon agents using self-generated summaries for turn-level credit assignment with intra-group rescaling. (2) We propose novel intra-group credit rescaling method that refines self-generated credit using both successful and failed rollouts. (3) We show that Self-Credit outperforms strong agentic RL baselines on long-horizon agentic tasks across multiple models at different scales.

sections.title: 3 Methods
sections.content: We present an approach that creates dense supervision signals from outcome rewards for long-horizon agentic RL using self-generated credit with intra-group rescaling via compaction. Our method, Self-Credit, combines three components: (1) the policy performs compaction by generating summaries of the interaction history, and the summaries cite important turns in the history as credit; (2) Intra-group rescaling refines this self-generated credit against the outcomes of other rollouts for the same prompt; (3) The rescaled credit is used to upweight the advantages of cited turns. Figure 2 illustrates Self-Credit.

sections.title: 3.4 Annealing the Weights
sections.content: The importance of exploration and exploitation varies across different stages of LLM post-training (Cui et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025). Since the rescaled weights can influence this balance, we design learning curriculum with an annealing schedule for the repeated-failure penalty weight wf . Stronger penalties early in training are intended to discourage repeatedly unsuccessful retrieval actions and stabilize search behaviors, while weaker penalties later allow more exploration.

sections.title: 4.2 Baselines
sections.content: We compare against the following zero-shot and agentic RL baselines. The main differences between SelfCredit and these baselines can be found in Table 1. (1) Zero-shot evaluation of the base model does not use context management; (2) GRPO is applied to the multi-turn setting without any context management or turn-level credit assignment; (3) GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) modifies group-based RL with turn-level credit assignment by re-grouping the same rollouts based on action states that are matched by repetitive actions. Turns sharing an identical environment observation are matched into groups, and within each group the action receives standardized additive advantage adjustment; (4) SUPO (Lu et al., 2025) is compactionaugmented RL baseline that implements rolling summarization with free-form summary and optimizes the uniform-credit objective. There is no citation instruction in the summarization prompt and no turn-level credit assignment; (5) ECHO (Xie et al., 2026) replaces free-form summarization in summarization-augmented RL with explicit turn selection: at each summarization, the policy emits selection over its turn history, and the selected turn memories are carried into the next context in place of summary. It routes token-level credit to the turns selected by the policy in successful rollouts.

sections.title: 4.3 Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: For BrowseComp-Plus, we follow Chen et al. (2025b); Xie et al. (2026) and use the Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025b) retriever and the BrowseComp-Plus static corpus index as the search engine during evaluation. We report LLM-as-a-judge accuracy, prompting separate Qwen3-32B judge to determine whether the model-generated answer is semantically equivalent to the ground-truth answer. For deep research tasks, we follow Li et al. (2026c) to use open web search API instead of the static engine during evaluation. We report LLM-as-a-judge accuracy as well with the rubric from Gupta et al. (2026). For both tasks, we use temperature = 0.7 for decoding.

We observe that without penalties for repeated turns cited by failed rollouts, Qwen3-8B model learns to search excessively, likely caused by over-optimizing for the credit boost, and fails to learn to commit to an answer. sections.title: 7 Related Work
sections.content: Agentic RL for long-horizon tasks. Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used to post-train LLM agents (Jin et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c), building on policy-gradient methods such as PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). In long-horizon tasks (Sun et al., 2026), growing interaction histories can exceed the context window, while sparse outcome rewards provide limited information about the contribution of individual actions (Wang and Ammanabrolu, 2025; Tang et al., 2026). Recent work addresses these challenges by using inference-time methods (Xu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026), incorporating context management systems (Li et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a; Kang et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026) or self-compaction capability (Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Cursor Research et al., 2026) into the policy model through RL. Our work leverages self-compaction for context management during training for long horizon tasks. Credit assignment under sparse outcome rewards. Prior work derives finer grained credit given sparse outcome rewards from several sources, including learned critics (Zhou et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025d; Shi et al., 2026), process reward models (Zhang et al., 2026b; Zeng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026), hindsight information conditioned on answers (Tan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b) and sampling (Choudhury, 2025; Zong et al., 2026), but these methods usually require additional rollouts or hindsight information not available in intermediate steps. Other methods reuse sampled rollouts to compare returns at similar states (Feng et al., 2025; He et al., 2026), or leverage confidence of the policy model (Wang et al., 2025a; Dong et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a). Compared with prior work, our method combines signals that exist in standard group-based RL methods with self-compaction and rescales them using group-level statistics.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Training long-horizon LLM agents with RLVR is challenging because outcome rewards provide very sparse learning signals over long trajectories. We introduced Self-Credit, an end-to-end agentic RL method that creates dense supervision signals from single sparse outcome reward through self-generated credit with intra-group rescaling. The policy model generates summaries with citations to critical turns during compaction, and these citations serve as self-generated credit. Self-Credit then refines this credit with intra-group rescaling, which compares cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt, and uses the rescaled credit weights to selectively strengthen the advantages of tokens in model-cited turns. Self-Credit outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines on challenging search QA and deep research tasks across models. These results suggest that self-generated signals can be utilized for effective credit assignment in long-horizon agentic RL.

sections.title: B Implementation Details
sections.content: B.1 Prompts and Instructions The summarization instruction used in our experiments is the following. B.1 Summarization Instruction As the LAST line INSIDE the <summary> block, cite ONLY the few assistant turns whose findings were decisive for solving the taskusually 2 to 5 turns, NEVER every turnwritten exactly in this format: the critical turns are: <comma-separated turn numbers>. Pick the real turn numbers yourself based on the interaction; do NOT copy the placeholder and do NOT list every turn. Number the assistant turns starting from 1 for the first assistant tool-calling turn shown in the context above; do not count tool responses, any earlier summary block, or this instruction. Citation format. We introduce simple format gating on the generated citations: the citation line cannot be empty, and we strip out-of-range citations. An invalid citation line leads to format error and makes the entire rollout receive reward of 0. Summary for the final segment. Because compaction is only triggered at certain thresholds, turns in short last segment might not get chance to be cited, creating systematic bias in the credit signal. Therefore, when rollout trajectory is complete with final answer, we force the model to generate an auxiliary summary of the final segment. This auxiliary summary is not context-replacing summary and is not included in j. 15 B.2 Turn Matching Intra-group rescaling requires deciding when cited turn in one Matching turns across rollouts by actions. rollout performs the same action as turn in other rollouts for the same prompt. As defined in Section 2, turn consists of thinking trace, an agentic action, and an observation from the environment. For the setting of long horizon agentic tasks, we focus on actions to match turns because LLM agents learn to perform the right actions during training. In the two settings below, instead of comparing the text of tool calls, which rarely repeats verbatim across rollouts, we identify each action by the evidence it retrieves from the environment. BrowseComp-Plus. On BrowseComp-Plus, the agent interacts with fixed document corpus through three tools: (1) Search takes natural-language query and returns ranked list of retrieved documents, each of which has document identifier (docid); (2) open_page takes docid and returns the full text of that document; (3) finish submits the final answer and ends the interaction. We do not match turns with finish calls. For turns that leverage the other 2 types of tools, we use the following matching rules: (1) search call is represented by the set of docids it returned. Within each prompt group, we match search turns by the overlap between the sets of retrieved docids. Two turns are matched if the Jaccard similarity of their sets of retrieved docids is at least 0.6; (2) For open_page, we match turns by the docid they opened , and two open_page turns match only if they opened the same document. Deep research tasks. For deep research tasks, the agent browses fixed web corpus with OpenResearch harness during training through four tools: (1) search takes natural-language query and returns the top 20 results as links; (2) open takes link id or cursor from an earlier observation and returns the page content with line numbers; (3) find takes text pattern and returns the lines in an opened page that match it; (4) finish submits the final answer and ends the interaction. Unlike on BrowseComp-Plus, the agent refers to pages through link ids (e.g., URLs) and cursors (location on the website) that are local to each rollout, making matching harder. Therefore, we identify each document by its docid in the OpenResearcher corpus, which the retriever returns as metadata hidden from the agent, instead of by links or cursors. As in BrowseComp-Plus, we do not match turns with finish calls, and we match search turns by the Jaccard similarity of their retrieved docids (at least 0.6) and open turns by the docid they opened. For find, two turns match if they found adjacent lines in the same document. Turn matching for other tasks. The matching rules above are instances of general recipe: task-specific function matches turns by the observations from those turns. Intra-group rescaling only needs these matches, so it can be applied unchanged to other agentic tasks once such function is defined. This recipe is related to anchor-state grouping in GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025), which groups steps across trajectories that start from the same environment state, using exact matching or similarity threshold over the state text. The difference lies in what is matched: GiGPO compares the states in which actions are taken, while Self-Credit compares the observations that cited actions obtain, which remains informative in open-ended environments where states rarely repeat. For example, in embodied tasks such as ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021), turn can be described by the object and receptacle it acts on (e.g., an object picked by the agent), together with whether the action succeeded. Independence Assumption In this work, we assume that different turns in rollout contribute independently to the outcome, which is an approximation: an open action depends on the search that surfaced the document, and late turn may only succeed because of evidence gathered earlier. We adopt the approximation because it keeps the comparison to counts over rollouts rather than over trajectory prefixes, which would rarely match.

Optimization. We use learning rate of 1 106 with constant schedule and asymmetric clipping with ϵlow = 0.20 and ϵhigh = 0.28. The loss is averaged over tokens, with no entropy bonus, no KL penalty in either the loss or the reward, and no critic. Batching. Each training step uses 256 trajectories, split into 8 optimizer updates. We use 16 prompts per step and 16 rollouts per prompt. Sequence lengths. The maximum prompt length is 4096 tokens and the maximum response length is 32768 tokens. The threshold for compaction is 16384 tokens. Rollouts. Rollouts are generated asynchronously in multi-turn agent loop, with tool calls in the Hermes format. Tool responses are truncated to 16K characters. The maximum number of assistant turns is 100. For BrowseComp-Plus, we allow the model to use 5 parallel tool calls and train for 115 steps, following the settings used by Xie et al. (2026). sections.title: D OOD Generalization
sections.content: D.1 Out-of-distribution Generalization To evaluate the out-of-distribution transfer of different methods to shorter horizon tasks after training on long horizon, we evaluate zero-shot transfer of the Qwen3-32B policies to four out-of-distribution search-augmented QA benchmarks, following prior work (Jin et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026). As shown in Table 7, Self-Credit achieves the highest average accuracy, 46.6%, compared with 45.4% for GRPO, 44.5% for ECHO, and 44.3% for SUPO. This demonstrates that tool use behaviors learned with long horizon training with Self-Credit generalize to shorter tasks as well.

sections.title: E Details of Analysis
sections.content: Tool-use quality metrics. BrowseComp-Plus annotates each question with gold documents, which contain the answer, and larger set of evidence documents, which are needed to support it. Gold Searched and Gold 17 Opened are the percentages of questions for which at least one gold document appeared in any search result or was opened, respectively. Answer Recall is the fraction of questions gold documents that the policy either retrieved or opened, averaged over questions, and Evidence Recall is the same quantity computed over evidence documents. (1) Opened and Searched. We measure whether the turns model cites Citation quality metrics in Table 6. contain the evidence needed for the answer, using the gold documents that BrowseComp-Plus annotates in the dataset. An Open or Search turn is considered important if it opened gold document (Opened ) or if one of its search results was gold document (Searched ). We compute the F1 of the cited turns against these turns, excluding the final answer turn. (2) LLM Judge. useful exploratory turn may not find any gold documents but still inform the model about what to do next. While these turns still provide learning signals, the metrics above might overlook such turns. Therefore, we use LLM Judge F1 to score model citations against turns that Claude Sonnet 4.6 labels as decisive or as finding new relevant information, which does not rely on gold annotations. We use the LLM-as-judge prompt from Xu et al. (2026). Rule firing and precision in Figure 4. We measure how often each intra-group rescaling rule scenario is applied during training and whether it is applied to the right turns. The firing rate is the fraction of cited turns on which rule is applied. The firing precision checks fired turns against turns that find the gold documents, i.e., turns that either opened gold document or if one of its search results was gold document. For the repeated success scenario, the firing precision is the share of fired turns that find gold documents. For repeated failure and mixed outcome, its precision is the share of fired turns that do not find gold documents.
